case_prompt:
A 32-year-old Caucasian man with an eight-year history of well-controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus (average blood glucose 150 mg/dL; hemoglobin A₁c 7.5%) presented with a three-month history of an unintended 22-pound weight loss. He denied abdominal pain, diarrhea, changes in diet or exercise, palpitations, heat intolerance, neck soreness, or other thyroid-related symptoms. His diabetes regimen (insulin pump plus pramlintide) and glycemic control were unchanged. 

On examination, he was well-nourished and in no distress. Blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg, pulse 72 beats/minute. There was no lid lag, proptosis, thyroid enlargement, tenderness, cervical lymphadenopathy, or tremor. 

Laboratory studies showed normal complete blood count, electrolytes, liver and kidney function. Thyroid studies revealed a suppressed TSH level of 0.033 mIU/L (reference 0.4–5.0 mIU/L) and a free thyroxine level of 33 pmol/L (reference 7.7–15.4 pmol/L). An anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody was elevated at 13.2 SD (normal <2.0 SD). A thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) assay was undetectable. Serum thyroglobulin was within the normal range.

sentences.text: A 32-year-old Caucasian man with an eight-year history of well-controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus (average blood glucose 150 mg/dL; hemoglobin A₁c 7.5%) presented with a three-month history of an unintended 22-pound weight loss.
He denied abdominal pain, diarrhea, changes in diet or exercise, palpitations, heat intolerance, neck soreness, or other thyroid-related symptoms.
His diabetes regimen (insulin pump plus pramlintide) and glycemic control were unchanged.
On examination, he was well-nourished and in no distress.
Blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg, pulse 72 beats/minute.
There was no lid lag, proptosis, thyroid enlargement, tenderness, cervical lymphadenopathy, or tremor.
Laboratory studies showed normal complete blood count, electrolytes, liver and kidney function.
Thyroid studies revealed a suppressed TSH level of 0.033 mIU/L (reference 0.4–5.0 mIU/L) and a free thyroxine level of 33 pmol/L (reference 7.7–15.4 pmol/L).
An anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody was elevated at 13.2 SD (normal <2.0 SD).
A thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) assay was undetectable.
Serum thyroglobulin was within the normal range.

diagnostic_reasoning: 1. Graves’ disease was unlikely given thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin was not detected — “the results of a thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) assay were undetectable.” 2. Thyrotoxicosis factitia was ruled out by a normal thyroglobulin level, which would be low in exogenous hormone use — “His serum thyroglobulin was normal, arguing against thyroid hormone self-administration (thyrotoxicosis factitia).” 3. Autoimmune thyroiditis best fit the findings, given high anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies and exclusion of other causes — “the diagnosis of autoimmune thyroiditis was made on the basis of the presence of anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies and the absence of evidence of another etiology for hyperthyroidism, such as Graves' disease, multi-nodular goiter or toxic adenoma.”

selection.screen_reason: Thyrotoxicosis with positive TPO, undetectable TSI and normal thyroglobulin supports thyrotoxic autoimmune thyroiditis; good negatives in the history.
selection.second_look_note: Unexplained weight loss in a type 1 diabetic with denied thyroid symptoms directs thyroid testing; positive TPO antibodies with undetectable TSI and normal thyroglobulin decide.
